cells.tense: Something is arriving now, and your feeling about it has had time to settle before you act on it.
cells.act: follow the thought past where it is comfortable
cells.ask: After something arrives — a message, a plan, a person — take your first read one step further than feels comfortable, and answer from there.
cells.core:
Something is coming toward you, and your feeling about it has already had its say — quietly, without drama. That steadiness is the point: the heart reads things before the thinking starts, and that read doesn't need to be argued into shape. It just needs a hearing.

The depth is where the useful thing lives. So when the next arrival shows up — a message, a plan, someone walking toward you — give it more than a glance. Follow it a while, let it show you its shape, and act from what you find underneath. The first read is fine; the pattern past it is better, and you're built to go there.
cells.sheetLine: Let what's arriving show itself before you answer it.
cells.verb: sitting with what the heart already knows while something new arrives
cells.place: the threshold where what was outside is entering now

cells.tense: You are already living past the moment something arrives, filling in what it will mean before it has landed.
cells.act: count what the ending gave you
cells.ask: When a new thing shows up, count what the last one gave you first — one honest thing — then meet what's arriving at whatever speed it comes.
cells.core:
Something is on its way in, and you're already three steps past it — rehearsing how it will go, what it will mean, what you'll do when it lands. The picture is so complete that the actual arrival barely gets a look. That's a mind that likes to be ready before the thing is here, and it has its reasons.

But you've been through endings before, and you know what they left you. When a new thing shows up, name what the last one gave you first — one honest thing. Then meet the arrival at whatever speed it comes. The bracing eases when you remember you've already been carried by something you didn't predict.
cells.sheetLine: You're meeting the arrival before it gets here.
cells.verb: sitting with what the heart already knows while something new arrives
cells.place: the threshold where what was outside is entering now

cells.tense: The connection you're waiting for already happened, and you're still parked at the point where it would have arrived.
cells.act: bring the two sides of your thinking into one plan
cells.ask: Wherever your thinking has split — about a person, a plan, yourself — put both sides on a page, and write the single plan that holds them.
cells.core:
Something wanted to come in, and the door stayed shut. You can feel the shape of the connection that didn't quite land — the warmth, the recognition, the thing that was almost here — and you're still near where it would have entered. The feeling itself is fine; it's the arrival that stalled.

What's scattered is not your heart but your thoughts about it. So do the small, unglamorous work: take one place where your thinking has split, put both sides on a page, and find the single line that holds them. That line is enough to stand on, and standing is how the next thing gets in. The feeling follows the alignment, not the other way around.
cells.sheetLine: The arrival stalled. Your thinking can still catch up.

cells.tense: Something is entering now, and the quiet depth you bring to it is being filed under someone else's name.
cells.act: let the mind find its own limit in the thing
cells.ask: When a hard thing comes your way, hold it past the first kind answer until your own read shows itself — and keep that read as yours.
cells.core:
Something is entering, and your way of meeting it is quiet — a long look, a settled feeling, no rush to say anything. People feel that from you. They call it listening, or being easy to talk to, or just the way you are. None of that is wrong; it just leaves out the part where the reading is happening on your side of the table.

The depth is yours and it works. The next time it opens, remain in it a beat longer than the conversation wants — past the first kind answer, into what you actually see. You don't have to announce it. Just don't hand it away. Naming it yours is the whole of the acknowledgment.
cells.sheetLine: The quiet depth is yours. You keep calling it listening.
cells.verb: sitting with what the heart already knows while something new arrives
cells.place: the threshold where what was outside is entering now

attempts.check: The draft's weakest claim is that the person is 'braced' against a feeling still forming — the record supports the seat (something entering now) and the status (running ahead of it), but not any particular thing they're bracing about, so the core must stay at the level of the capacity, not the content. A reader could reasonably say the arrival is welcome and they're simply excited, which is why Too Much is written as the accounting running ahead of the thing rather than fear of it. The asks survive a wrong read: each is the medicine's own act done small on whoever or whatever is at the door, useful whether the person is braced, eager, or numb. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person is any phrasing of 'you're afraid to let it in' — that's cut; the record says the capacity runs ahead, not that it's scared.
